       INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS’ MOTION FOR LEAVE TO
      ANSWER AND ANSWER TO THE ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION,
                                L.L.C.

          Pursuant to Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 the

Indicated PJM Transmission Owners 2 respectfully move for leave to submit this answer in

response to the answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) filed on September 10, 2026.3

          This proposed answer addresses a narrow but important issue: whether it violates cost-

causation principles to impose new exit fees related to a generation/capacity product on a

transmission owner (“TO”) as opposed to a load-serving entity (“LSE”). PJM’s answer does

not confront that issue or the arguments raised by the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners in

their initial protest in the instant proceeding. PJM does, however, concede that the cause of




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2026).
2
  The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are American Transmission Systems, Inc., Mid-Atlantic
Interstate Transmission, LLC, Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company, Keystone Appalachian
Transmission Company, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Monongahela Power Company, and
The Potomac Edison Company (collectively, “The FirstEnergy Transmission Companies”), and
Duquesne Light Company.
3
  See Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-
3380-000 (Sept. 10, 2026) (“PJM Answer”).
 the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) is loads (served by LSEs). 4 And, thus, any and

all costs associated with the RBP must be borne by LSEs, and not TOs.

          Accordingly, the Commission should not allow the RBP to go into effect without

removing its Exit Amendment that imposes exit fees on TOs.

I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          Just as the Commission’s rules do not permit as of right PJM’s proposed answer to the

various protests in this Docket, they do not permit as of right the Indicated PJM Transmission

Owners’ proposed answer to PJM’s proposed answer. 5 The Commission nonetheless retains

authority to permit such an answer in its discretion. The Commission should do so here

because the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed answer highlights an important

concession in PJM’s proposed answer that bears on cost-causation principles that PJM

otherwise does not address.

II.       PROPOSED ANSWER

          The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ protest explained that, under cost-causation

principles and the Commission’s precedent applying them, RBP-related exit fees cannot be

imposed on TOs as opposed to LSEs: “The Commission has never allocated generation- and

capacity-related costs to TOs and, more specifically, the Exit Amendment [of the RBP]

conflicts with highly relevant precedent in the Duquesne Light Co. proceeding where the




4
  PJM Answer at 86 (“Given that the RBP is to address the capacity shortfall from the 2027/2028 and
2028/2029 RPM Auctions, which is primarily driven by the unprecedented addition of large loads (in
the form of Load Adjustments), the loads causing the RBP—through their LSEs—should bear the costs
of the RBP Resources throughout the full term.”) (emphasis added).
5
     See 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).


                                                2
 Commission notably did not apply generation-related costs to an exiting TO in its capacity as

a TO,” but only in its capacity as an LSE.6

         PJM’s answer does not address this argument or the relevant portion of Duquesne Light

Company.7 It does, however, concede that loads and LSEs are the causes of the RBP: “Given

that the RBP is to address the capacity shortfall from the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 RPM

Auctions, which is primarily driven by the unprecedented addition of large loads (in the form

of Load Adjustments), the loads causing the RBP—through their LSEs—should bear the costs

of the RBP Resources throughout the full term.” 8 (emphasis added).

         PJM does not and cannot explain how it is consistent with Duquesne Light Company

and cost-causation principles to impose RBP exit fees on a TO as opposed to an LSE. At a

minimum, therefore, even if all of the RBP’s other deficiencies could be overlooked, the

Commission should strip out the exit fee provision before the RBP is allowed to go into effect.

III.     CONCLUSION

         For the foregoing reasons, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners respectfully

request that the Commission accept this answer and reject PJM’s proposed Exit Amendment.
